body.heading: Rivers that gave and took away
paragraphs: Mesopotamia means 'the land between the rivers' — the Tigris and Euphrates, in what is now Iraq. The rivers flooded unpredictably, sometimes ruining crops, but they also laid down rich soil, and farmers who learned to channel water into canals could grow far more food than a family needed.

Surplus food changed everything. When some people could be fed by others' farming, they could become potters, priests, soldiers, scribes — specialists. Specialists need organising, and organising needs a centre. That centre became the city.

body.heading: Uruk, the first great city
paragraphs: By around 3300 BC, the city of Uruk may have held tens of thousands of people, ringed by a wall its legends credited to the hero-king Gilgamesh. Its temples rose on stepped towers, and its workshops produced pottery, metalwork and textiles on an industrial scale.

City life created a new problem: how to keep track of grain, livestock, labour and trade. The solution, developed in these cities, was writing — wedge-shaped marks called cuneiform, pressed into wet clay with a cut reed.

body.heading: Ideas that never left
paragraphs: From Mesopotamia came habits we still live by: dividing the hour into 60 minutes and the circle into 360 degrees, keeping written laws, lending at interest, and telling stories of a great flood and a hero seeking eternal life.
The first cities were experiments that worked. Everything since — including the city you may be reading this in — is a variation on their theme.

takeaway: Between the Tigris and Euphrates, irrigation farming created food surpluses, specialists and cities — and writing was invented to keep count.
